text: Retain hardware watchdog, softlockup, hung-task and NMI detection and wire them to the service supervisor and the crash-capture path.
Decide eBPF's native role (tracing substrate, sched_ext, network policy) and whether the Linux personality exposes bpf() beyond a CAP_BPF-equivalent capability.
Decide that kernel live-patching is a non-goal: system generations plus reboot are the update model.
Adopt an ADR fixing the license for all new native kernel code, with options GPLv2-only, GPLv2-or-later, and dual GPLv2/MIT for reusable abstractions.
rationale: Code linked into a GPLv2 kernel must be GPLv2-compatible, and the choice decides whether kernel-side abstractions can ever be shared with permissive userspace.

text: Define the out-of-tree and proprietary kernel module policy for the fork: whether native kernel objects are exported GPL-only, module signing enforcement and taint semantics.
rationale: Vendors and users will ask whether they can load third-party modules and the answer must be settled before the native ABI stabilizes.

text: Honor MODULE_LICENSE and GPL-only symbol semantics unchanged for inherited Linux modules under the fork.
rationale: Inherited drivers must behave identically or hardware support silently changes legal status.

text: Adopt an upstream-first policy for the Linux-derived hardware layer: driver and subsystem fixes go to upstream Linux before or alongside the fork.
rationale: It keeps the divergence surface small and preserves goodwill needed when adapting upstream changes.

text: Maintain a divergence ledger classifying every fork patch as upstream-candidate, fork-only or temporary, with rebase status, exposed as a generated report.
rationale: Controlled divergence is only controlled if every patch is accounted for.

text: Decide the upstream base to track (LTS versus mainline), rebase cadence, and the measurable criteria that trigger the Phase D transition to controlled divergence.
rationale: The kernel evolution phases need objective triggers rather than judgment calls.

text: Set kernel identity conventions (uname strings, version scheme, bug-report routing) so the fork is never reported to upstream Linux as Linux.
rationale: Misrouted bug reports damage the upstream relationship and confuse users.

text: Define the relationship with Rust-for-Linux: contribute reusable abstractions upstream and set a policy for Rust toolchain version pinning relative to upstream's minimum.
rationale: Diverging Rust kernel infrastructure would forfeit the largest source of future safe-abstraction work.

text: Zero unclassified fork patches and full SBOM coverage are required at every milestone gate.
rationale: Compliance debt compounds and gates are the only enforcement point.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Maintain kernel configuration as a base defconfig plus per-target fragments (QEMU minimal, QEMU desktop, each reference machine) with a CI check that every fragment still builds and boots.
rationale: Uncontrolled CONFIG drift is the most common way a kernel fork breaks hardware it previously supported.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Adopt KUnit plus Rust kernel unit tests and doctests for all native primitives, run on every pre-merge build under QEMU.
rationale: Capability derivation, channel semantics and operation lifecycles need fast in-kernel unit coverage before integration tests are viable.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build an upstream-tracking bot that attempts merges of each upstream Linux stable and mainline tag into the fork, reports conflicts by subsystem, and runs the boot matrix on the result.
rationale: §6 Phase D adaptation of upstream changes needs continuous visibility of divergence cost or merges stop happening.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Test nested virtualisation and the retained KVM path in CI so JakeOS can host VMs, including running its own test harness inside a guest.
rationale: KVM is listed as preserved in §5 and preservation claims need tests.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Decide how the fork responds when upstream Linux raises its minimum Rust version or stabilises features the fork's Rust code depends on, including whether to track upstream's minimum or pin independently.
rationale: Diverging toolchain requirements from upstream make Phase D driver adaptation progressively more expensive.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Require all kernel-resident code (modules, firmware blobs loaded by drivers) to be signed and rejected when unsigned under Secure Boot.
rationale: Verifying the kernel image while loading unsigned modules leaves the chain of trust open at the most privileged layer.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Define and maintain a kernel hardening configuration baseline (KASLR, stack protector, kCFI, SMEP/SMAP, IBT, shadow stacks, init_on_alloc/free, hardened usercopy, W^X, randomized freelists) tracked as a checked-in config with CI enforcement.
rationale: The fork inherits Linux's defaults, which are tuned for compatibility rather than a desktop that promises capability-grade security.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Prune the kernel attack surface for the constrained target hardware: disable unused legacy drivers, obsolete filesystems, unneeded protocols and syscalls not required by the native ABI or the Linux personality.
rationale: §62 deliberately limits target hardware, which makes a minimal kernel configuration achievable and removes whole classes of CVEs.

text: Define the kernel module signing policy covering out-of-tree modules, proprietary GPU drivers and locally built modules under Secure Boot.
rationale: NVIDIA users and kernel developers both need a sanctioned path that does not require disabling Secure Boot.

text: Decide the upstream Linux tracking cadence: which upstream LTS series to base on, rebase frequency per divergence phase, and automation for stable-branch backports.
rationale: Fork maintenance cost and CVE exposure are determined by this policy from the first commit.

text: Build a CVE ingestion pipeline that pulls kernel CNA and upstream advisories, auto-tags applicability against forked or removed subsystems, and opens triage tasks.
rationale: The kernel CNA issues thousands of CVEs a year and manual triage of a fork will not scale.

text: Capture kernel panics into persistent storage (pstore/kdump) and submit them after the next successful boot.
rationale: Kernel fork regressions are the highest-severity failures and are otherwise invisible to developers.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Select the Linux base version and LTS alignment for the fork and decide the upstream tracking strategy (periodic rebase vs merge) with a measured rebase cost after the first six months.
rationale: Fork maintenance is a permanent cost and the tracking strategy determines when Phase D divergence becomes affordable.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Run a Rust-in-kernel viability spike identifying which Linux internal subsystems (mm, scheduler, DRM, VFS) need new Rust abstractions for the native platform, and decide the C-versus-Rust boundary.
rationale: Rust-first is stated policy but the binding gap to Linux internals is unknown and dictates early velocity.

text: Decide the kernel strategy as a radical fork of the Linux kernel (ADR: fork vs new microkernel vs Linux-as-hypervisor), recording the rationale of hardware maturity vs native model.
Do not pursue a traditional microkernel for academic purity; kernel residency of subsystems is decided by measured cost, not ideology.
Do not rewrite the kernel for the sake of rewriting it; every rewrite task must cite a semantic or measured benefit.
The OS must inherit Linux's mature hardware foundation while not inheriting Linux as the native programming model.
Retain Linux virtualization support (KVM) in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux x86-64 architecture support in the forked kernel.
Do not remove or break Linux ARM64 architecture support in the fork even though ARM64 is not an initial platform; keep a future port possible.
Do not remove or break Linux RISC-V architecture support in the fork; keep a future port possible.
Do not replace a mature subsystem merely because it is old.
Preserve Linux page-table management as a mechanism the native memory model builds upon.
Preserve Linux memory allocators (page allocator, slab) as native mechanisms.
Preserve Linux interrupt handling infrastructure unchanged in the fork.
Kernel Core owns memory management as a native kernel responsibility.
A Linux-derived hardware layer (drivers, buses) sits beneath the kernel core and is retained from upstream.
ADR: which services are user-space (UI, Storage, Network) vs kernel core (Memory, IPC, Capabilities, Scheduler), with criteria for moving a service across the boundary.
ADR: select the contemporary Linux kernel version and tree (mainline vs LTS) to fork, with rebase cadence.
Create the kernel fork repository with upstream remote, patch tracking and a documented rebase workflow.
Preserve Linux architecture support code in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux interrupt subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux memory-management internals in the fork initially.
Preserve KVM in the fork initially.
Do not attempt a heroic kernel rewrite; the V0 objective is adding the native model alongside retained Linux facilities.
Phase A: keep the fork reasonably close to upstream while adding the native platform alongside Linux facilities.
ADR: Phase D entry criteria—when full upstream merges stop being mandatory and controlled divergence begins.
Phase D: process for adapting upstream driver improvements into the diverged kernel.
Phase D: process for adapting upstream security fixes (CVE backport pipeline) into the diverged kernel.
Phase D: process for adapting upstream architecture improvements into the diverged kernel.
Phase D: process for adopting upstream algorithms, scheduler ideas and memory-management improvements selectively.
Phase D: process for adapting upstream subsystem patches rather than blind merging.
Phase E: reach a kernel no longer reasonably described as Linux, with independent native ABI, execution model, security model, IPC architecture and system semantics.
Write and maintain the kernel divergence policy document defining phases A–E, their gates and what upstream tracking each phase requires.
Build upstream-tracking tooling that reports patch delta, conflict hot-spots and unmerged upstream security fixes.
Decide the initial implementation of ResourceDomain as a wrapper over cgroups v2 controllers (cpu, memory, io, pids) per §6 Phase C, and record the migration path to a native implementation.
Decide the phase at which the Linux personality moves from direct kernel syscall ABI to a translation layer over native primitives, mapped to kernel phases B–D (§6) (ADR).
All new kernel and platform code must be Rust-first.
Inherited mature Linux C code is retained where rewriting provides insufficient value.
Write the rewrite-versus-retain policy defining criteria for replacing inherited C with Rust.
Keep inherited Linux hardware support working for as long as possible; no native feature may ship if it regresses inherited driver functionality on reference hardware.
Do not destabilise the DRM subsystem while building the native platform.
Do not destabilise the PCI subsystem while building the native platform.
Do not destabilise the USB subsystem while building the native platform.
Do not destabilise the NVMe/block subsystem while building the native platform.
Do not destabilise networking drivers or the network stack while building the native platform.
Do not destabilise ACPI while building the native platform.
GPU driver update process that tracks upstream amdgpu/i915/xe/nouveau fixes into the fork (cross-ref §56.4).
CVE response process for the forked kernel: triage, upstream patch identification, backport, testing, disclosure timeline.
Driver adaptation process and tooling for pulling upstream driver changes into the fork after divergence.
Subsystem maintenance ownership map assigning an owner to every inherited Linux subsystem retained in the fork.
Architecture support maintenance plan (x86-64 now; ARM64 and RISC-V potential) with per-architecture CI.
Hardware enablement process for supporting new devices after upstream merges become non-mandatory.
ADR: upstream tracking cadence and divergence policy for each kernel evolution phase A–E (cross-ref §6), including when full merges stop.
Do not rewrite every Linux subsystem; each rewrite requires an ADR showing meaningful benefit.
Do not move everything to userspace for ideological microkernel purity.
Do not preserve upstream mergeability at the expense of the architecture.
Study Linux for mechanisms to retain (scheduler, mm, block, net, drivers) and semantics to replace; produce a retained-mechanism inventory.
Study Redox OS for Rust-in-kernel practices, scheme-based resources and lessons from a Rust microkernel.
Study macOS/XNU Mach ports, launchd service activation and the app sandbox/entitlements model.
KVM retained in the kernel and exposed to native software as a capability-mediated virtualization object.
Decide how KVM/virtualization is exposed natively (e.g. Capability<VirtualMachine>) and whether compatibility personalities may fall back to VMs for unsupported software.
Defining technical strategy: use Linux for everything Linux is exceptionally good at; document the retained-mechanism list and review it at each milestone.
